Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.

We represent: petitioner.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an agency acts arbitrarily and capriciously when it departs from prior policy without acknowledging the change and offering a reasoned explanation.

Cite at least six decisions of the D.C. Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

Before you cite anything, call find_authority with the proposition and the circuit: it returns real cases that courts have cited for it, in the courts' own words, and that circuit's own F.3d opinions saying so. Cite from those results rather than from memory.

**ARGUMENT**

**I. [Agency]'s Unacknowledged and Unexplained Change in Policy Is Arbitrary and Capricious.**

The Administrative Procedure Act requires a court to set aside agency action that is "arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law." 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). To survive that review, an agency must examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action, including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made. *Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n of U.S., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.*, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983). [Agency]'s [Order] fails that standard. It abandons [prior policy] without saying so and without explaining why.

**A. An agency must acknowledge a change in policy and justify it.**

Agencies may change course, but not silently. An agency ordinarily must "display awareness that it *is* changing position," may not "depart from a prior policy *sub silentio* or simply disregard rules that are still on the books," and must show that there are good reasons for the new policy. *FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc.*, 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009). It need not prove that the new policy is better than the old one. It must, however, provide a more detailed justification when, for example, its new policy rests on factual findings that contradict those underlying the prior policy, or when the prior policy has engendered serious reliance interests. *Id.* at 515–16; *see also State Farm*, 463 U.S. at 42 (requiring reasoned analysis when an agency changes course by rescinding a rule).

This Court enforces that obligation consistently. When an agency departs from longstanding practices and official policies, it "must at a minimum acknowledge the change and offer a reasoned explanation for it." *Am. Wild Horse Pres. Campaign v. Perdue*, 873 F.3d 914, 923 (D.C. Cir. 2017). Reasoned decisionmaking requires the agency to confront its departure from established precedent and adequately explain it. *Dillmon v. Nat'l Transp. Safety Bd.*, 588 F.3d 1085, 1089–90 (D.C. Cir. 2009). A departure lacking that explanation is arbitrary and capricious and cannot stand. *ANR Pipeline Co. v. FERC*, 71 F.3d 897, 901 (D.C. Cir. 1995); *see also Williams Gas Processing–Gulf Coast Co. v. FERC*, 475 F.3d 319, 326 (D.C. Cir. 2006) (an agency changing its course must supply a reasoned analysis).

The same rule forbids treating like cases differently without justification. *W. Deptford Energy, LLC v. FERC*, 766 F.3d 10, 20 (D.C. Cir. 2014). Nor may an agency simply ignore contrary decisions. An agency's "failure to come to grips with conflicting precedent constitutes 'an inexcusable departure from the essential requirement of reasoned decision making.'" *Ramaprakash v. FAA*, 346 F.3d 1121, 1130 (D.C. Cir. 2003) (citation omitted); *accord Jicarilla Apache Nation v. U.S. Dep't of the Interior*, 613 F.3d 1112, 1120 (D.C. Cir. 2010).

**B. [Agency] neither acknowledged nor explained its departure.**

For [period], [Agency] adhered to [describe prior policy, with record and precedent citations]. The [Order] adopts the opposite position: [describe new position, with record citations]. Yet it nowhere acknowledges that [Agency] has changed its position. [Address any passing reference to the prior policy and explain why it is inadequate.] That omission alone is fatal. *See Fox*, 556 U.S. at 515; *Am. Wild Horse*, 873 F.3d at 923.

Nor does the [Order] supply good reasons for the change. [Identify the missing or conclusory reasoning; any contrary factual findings left unaddressed; and Petitioner's reliance interests, with record citations showing they were raised before the agency.] Because [Agency] did not recognize that it was changing course, it never weighed what that change would cost those who relied on the prior policy.

Appellate counsel cannot repair these defects. A court may not accept counsel's *post hoc* rationalizations or supply a reasoned basis that the agency itself did not give. *State Farm*, 463 U.S. at 43, 50. The [Order] must be judged on its own explanation, and it offers none adequate to the departure. The Court should grant the petition, vacate the [Order], and remand.
